Dear Senator Welch,

Wait, so you're basically admitting you've done NOTHING to fix this in your own state? And you're also - maybe accidentally? - confessing that the ACA is completely BROKEN? Oh, and here's the part where you conveniently forget WHO actually voted to end those COVID ACA subsidies. Let me help you out here... it was THE DEMOCRATS!

Literally not one single Republican voted to END those temporary COVID relief subsidies. Think about that for a second. YOUR party cooked up this temporary sugar rush with the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 and the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, then just let it expire, and now you're acting shocked - SHOCKED! - about the utterly predictable consequences? It's like going to your boss and saying "Hey, last month you gave me a $1000 Christmas bonus, so this month when you didn't give me another thousand dollars, you basically CUT MY PAY! Where's your heart?!"

Here's what really gets me about your theatrical hand-wringing, Senator. That $415 you're so concerned about? I pay MORE than that as a TEACHER with supposedly "good" UNION-NEGOTIATED, EMPLOYER-ASSISTED healthcare! So you're seriously asking taxpayers to cough up $1.5 TRILLION so someone making $50,000 can pay less for insurance than educators who supposedly have premium benefits already pay?

Okay, let's talk about that $1.5 trillion price tag for a minute because the numbers are genuinely mind-blowing. If you stacked one-dollar bills, you'd reach about 102,000 MILES HIGH. That's not a typo - 408 TIMES TALLER THAN MOUNT EVEREST, which would get you almost HALFWAY TO THE MOON. Laid end to end? Those dollars would wrap around the EARTH'S EQUATOR 5,884 TIMES. Here's the part that really matters though: $1.5 trillion breaks down to $18,750 PER TAXPAYER. Or to put it more accurately, that's $18,750 we're adding to the debt for EVERY SINGLE PERSON.

So forgive me if I'm not exactly moved by your argument that we absolutely must spend nearly NINETEEN THOUSAND DOLLARS per taxpayer so that someone can save $145 per month compared to what they'd pay without the temporary COVID subsidies that - and I can't stress this enough - YOUR OWN PARTY voted to end.

You know what's really something? The logic pretzel you're twisting yourself into here. On one hand, the ACA works great (except when you admit it doesn't). On the other hand, without massive subsidies it's totally unaffordable (which kinda proves it doesn't work). THEN you claim Republicans are heartless for not extending YOUR temporary subsidies that YOU let expire. AND FINALLY, taxpayers should just cover all these costs instead of asking the uncomfortable question of why healthcare got so ridiculously expensive under YOUR signature legislation in the first place.

This is textbook QUINN'S SECOND LAW in action: "Liberals use the carnage of their policies to advance their ideology." You built an unsustainable system, pumped it full of temporary subsidies to hide the real costs, let those subsidies expire right on schedule, and now you're weaponizing the resulting price increases to demand permanent taxpayer funding at $18,750 per person. Brilliant strategy, terrible policy.

Here's a thought experiment. What if - and I know this sounds crazy - instead of throwing $1.5 trillion at subsidizing an admittedly broken system, we actually addressed WHY healthcare costs went through the roof after the ACA passed? Remember Obama's famous promise that the average family would save $2,500 per year? Yeah, my family's still waiting for that check to show up.

The reality you keep dancing around is pretty straightforward. The ACA created a system where insurance companies get guaranteed profits, young healthy people are legally required to subsidize older sicker people through community rating mandates, and actual healthcare costs just keep climbing because there's literally zero incentive for price competition anywhere in the system. You're not defending healthcare access here, Senator - you're defending a corporatist wealth transfer from regular taxpayers to insurance company shareholders.

Let's address the massive elephant stomping around in this room. If the ACA is truly the phenomenal success you claim it is, why exactly does it require PERMANENT subsidies totaling $1.5 TRILLION just to keep premiums "affordable"? That's not what success looks like - that's what life support for a fundamentally failed policy looks like, and you absolutely refuse to admit it doesn't work.

So before you lecture anyone in Nebraska about premium increases, maybe take a minute to explain to your own constituents why they should trust the party that promised healthcare savings but delivered massive cost increases, created temporary subsidies while knowing they'd expire, voted to end those subsidies themselves, and now demands taxpayers spend $18,750 each to patch the problem they created?

I've got a better idea. How about we actually repeal and replace the ACA with a system that brings down costs instead of endlessly subsidizing inflated ones? Health Savings Accounts paired with catastrophic coverage, real interstate competition, actual price transparency requirements, and ending the employer-based insurance tax benefit that distorts the entire market - THOSE reforms would do infinitely more to help that 31-year-old Nebraskan than throwing another $1.5 trillion in subsidies at a broken system.

But that would require admitting the ACA failed. And we both know you'd rather bankrupt the entire country than admit that uncomfortable truth.

What counts as climate-tax in WA: Climate Commitment Act (CCA)
•The main policy is the CCA, a “cap-and-invest” program passed in 2021.  
•Under the CCA, large emitters of greenhouse gases (e.g., power plants, refineries, big industry) must buy “allowances” for each metric ton of CO₂ (or equivalent) they release.  
•The total number of allowances is gradually reduced over time (“cap”), forcing polluters to cut emissions or pay for allowances; over time this should reduce emissions significantly.  

💲 What the “tax” looks like in practice
•Although the CCA doesn’t directly tax retail fuel or electricity, the increased cost to businesses tends to be passed on to consumers — so many people feel a resulting “climate-tax effect.”  
•As of recent allowance auctions, prices have been rising: e.g. one recent auction settled at about $50 per metric ton CO₂, up from earlier values.  
•Those allowance prices are often translated into approximate impacts on gasoline and diesel prices: for example, one analysis put the cost of the CO₂ tax at around $0.46 per gallon of gasoline, or $0.56 per gallon of diesel at that time.  
•In 2023, a typical price was estimated around $54.74 per metric ton, equating to roughly $0.43 per gallon of gas (and $0.53/gal diesel).  

🏛️ What the tax revenue gets used for

The state does not just collect the money — a core feature of the CCA is reinvestment:  
•Over the 2023–2025 biennium, the state invested over $1.5 billion of CCA revenue.  
•According to the state, more than $330 million of that is expected to directly reduce greenhouse gas emissions — at a calculated cost of roughly $40 per metric ton of CO₂ reduced.  
•Other spending goes to climate resilience, clean-energy infrastructure (e.g. EV charging, clean transit), air-quality improvements, community health and, in many cases, targeting more vulnerable or overburdened communities.  

📉 What’s been the political / public reaction & recent developments
•In November 2024, voters in Washington rejected Initiative 2117 — a proposed repeal of the CCA program.  
•After the repeal effort failed, allowance prices increased significantly — which supporters say restores stability in the carbon market and ensures continued revenue for climate programs.  
•However, critics argue the CCA (or “CO₂ tax,” as some call it) has added to energy and fuel costs for households, especially as allowance prices rise.
